title: Planning a First Whisky Release | Craft Beer School
desc: How a craft distillery plans its first whisky release in India: choosing casks, strength, labels, registrations, price and timing.
teaser: A first release happens once. The casks, the strength and the label you choose will be judged for years.
standfirst: A distillery's first whisky is its introduction to the world. It sets expectations for everything that follows. Planning it starts long before bottling day, with cask choices, stock decisions and approvals that take months.
sections: Decide what the first release is for

Before picking casks, decide what the release must do. Some first releases aim for attention: a small, older, premium bottling that critics and collectors notice. Others aim for steady sales: a larger batch at a price more people can pay. Both are valid. Trying to do both with one release usually does neither well.

The answer shapes everything else: how many casks, which ones, the strength, the price and how many bottles. A small first release also protects stock for later expressions. Our guide to whisky inventory planning covers how to balance releases against what you hold.
Choose the casks by nose, not by date

The oldest casks are not always the best. In Indian heat, casks mature at different rates depending on their position in the warehouse, their size and their previous contents. Two casks filled on the same day can taste very different after three years.

Sample every candidate cask, reduce each sample to around 20% ABV with water and nose them side by side. Score them for the character you want. Look out for over-extracted wood, which shows as bitter tannin or heavy dryness. Watch too for casks that still taste immature. Then build a trial blend in small volumes, often 100 ml. Refine it before committing whole casks.

Bottling strength changes taste. Scotch must be at least 40% ABV. Much Indian whisky is sold at around 42.8%. Many craft releases sit at 46% or higher, often without chill filtration, which keeps more texture and flavour but can cause haze at low temperatures. Cask strength releases go out undiluted.

Run trial reductions at two or three strengths and taste them blind. Reduce in stages rather than all at once, using demineralised water, because hard water can cause haze. Decide on chill filtration based on the trial results and what your drinkers expect.

Label rules are strict and they vary. Any age statement must be the age of the youngest whisky in the bottle. Category terms such as single malt have definitions you must meet. Mandatory label information typically includes strength, volume, the manufacturer's details and statutory warnings set by food safety and excise rules.

Each label must usually be registered with the excise department in each state where you plan to sell. The price must be approved too. This takes time, often months. Start the registrations well before bottling. Check the current requirements with your licensing adviser. Our guide to designing a premium whisky label and bottle covers the design side.

Custom bottles, closures, labels and gift boxes all have lead times. Minimum order quantities can be far larger than a small first release needs. A custom glass mould can take many months. Many craft distilleries use a stock bottle with a distinctive label for the first release and move to a custom bottle once volumes justify it.

Order packaging after label approval, not before. A rejected label means reprinting.

Price comes from the full cost of the whisky, including years of storage, losses to evaporation, casks, packaging and the duties and margins along the route to market in each state. Excise duty and pricing structures differ widely between states, so the same bottle may sell at very different prices in neighbouring markets.

Plan the launch around the trade first: bartenders, retailers and writers who will talk about the whisky. Remember that direct advertising of alcohol is not allowed in India, so launches rely on events, tastings and word of mouth. Keep tastings responsible, with small measures, water and food.

Before the release goes to the bottling line, run a final set of checks on the blended batch. Measure strength with temperature correction and confirm it matches the label. Chill a sample to around 4 °C and look for haze, especially if the whisky is not chill filtered. Check colour against a reference sample so later batches can be matched.

Nose and taste the final batch with more than one person, ideally blind against the trial blend you approved. Keep retained samples from the batch, sealed and labelled, for at least as long as the product is on sale.

These checks take a day or two. Skipping them risks a release that hazes on a cold shelf or tastes different from what you approved. Our guide to whisky stability testing before release covers the haze side in more detail.

Write a one page release plan: purpose, number of bottles, target strength, casks in the running, states for launch and the date you need label approval by. Work backwards from your launch date and mark each approval and order. If cask selection or reduction feels uncertain, that is the skill to build before the casks are chosen.
faqs: How do distilleries choose casks for a first release?
By sampling every candidate cask, reducing samples to around 20% ABV, nosing them side by side and building small trial blends before committing whole casks.
What strength should a first whisky release be?
It depends on the style. Scotch must be at least 40% ABV. Many craft releases sit at 46% or higher. Taste trial reductions blind before deciding.
How long does label registration take in India?
It varies by state and often takes months. Start well before bottling and check current requirements with a licensing adviser.
